course_info.course_name: Horror Cinema and the Human Condition

course_details.Topic: Horror Cinema and the Human Condition
course_details.Overview of class:
In the twenty-first century, interest in horror has grown immensely in terms of
audience viewership, critical acclaim, and academic engagement creating larger discussions
around the genre's enjoyability and how it expresses socio-cultural fears and anxieties. Jordan
Peele's Get Out (2016), David Robert Mitchell's It Follows (2014), James Wan's Malignant
(2021) and Coralie Fargeat's The Substance (2024) are just a few examples of horror films that
simultaneously sparked renewed interest in the genre as entertainment and socio-cultural
conversations about race, sexuality, gender, class, and ability. Namely, how the unique technical
and textual conventions of the horror genre lend themselves to critiques of social movements and
identities in ways that other genres are unable or unwilling to attend to. The course will ask
students to contend broadly with the following questions: how do we account for the genre's
enduring cinematic popularity? How are contemporary horror films making inroads toward
understanding underrepresented historical, environmental, cultural and political perspectives?
What new fears and anxieties are being presented in the horror genre through contemporary
cinema?
course_details.Learning Objectives:
In this course, students will view a wide selection of contemporary horror
films ranging from slasher flicks, creature features, dark comedies, paranormal thrillers, found
footage films among other horror subcategories that show the genre's depth and versatility.
Through readings that explore the horror's history and traditional conventions, as well as
theoretical interventions made through gender & sexuality studies, feminist studies, disability
studies, and race studies, students will learn to critically engage with the textual and paratexual
elements of the genre. Students will demonstrate their grasp on new concepts through in-class
socratic discussion, weekly critiques of screenings, a short form presentation on one
screening/reading, a final project prospectus, and a final project which can consist of a traditional
paper, a video essay, a zine, or a creative art piece with an artist statement.
course_details.Class Materials (Required): All readings and screenings will be provided via Canvas.

course_details.Overview of class:
This course surveys the history of international cinema from its emergence through the 1950s. We will explore the diverse forms cinema took and functions it performed during this period by looking closely at a range of films and writings about them. We will examine the industrial, social, and historical contexts within which these films were produced and experienced as well as theorizations of cinema that emerged concurrently with them. The course thus introduces students to the study of film history as well as to key national and international trends in making and thinking about cinema as it rose to prominence as a vital component of the art and culture of the twentieth century.

Topics covered include the cinema of attractions; cinema's relation to colonialism; the development of narrative filmmaking; studio systems; audiences; exhibition practices; the concept of national cinemas as exemplified by the cinemas of the United States, France, Germany, the Soviet Union, Japan, India, and China; the avant-garde and cinema's relation to art movements; the coming of synchronized sound; animation; documentary cinema; and diverse conceptualizations of cinema's political possibilities and dangers.

course_details.Overview of class: This class will explore fundamental questions in the art and theory of nonfiction cinema. Students will view a range of observational, engaged, experimental, personal, industrial and commercial films from across the 130-year history of the medium, surveying acknowledged landmarks alongside under-recognized outliers and contemporary works. The course materials (including an intensive in-class screening schedule as well as visits from guest filmmakers, curators, and critics) will situate documentary within a spectrum encompassing narrative, avant-garde, and non-theatrical approaches to film. Readings and discussions will examine the material, formal, ethical, and political conditions of production and reception, paying close attention to questions of technology and environment and applying feminist and decolonial frameworks to prevailing narratives. Students will be asked to maintain consistent attendance, produce regular response papers, lead discussion around films and texts, and produce a final research paper or a final media arts project.

course_details.Learning Objectives: Engaged students will emerge from this class as more receptive, sensitive, and informed viewers of films from across the global history of nonfiction cinema. The course aims to provide the tools for close analysis, critical comparison, and constructive discussion of media; to create a space for informed and respectful debate of challenging and often imperfect objects; and to empower students to advance their own perspectives and to envision new futures for documentary film.

course_details.Overview of class: What does it mean to call a filmmaker an auteur? This course explores the history, affordances, and limitations of auteur theory through the films of Paul Thomas Anderson. Examining Anderson's distinctive visual style, recurring themes, collaborations, and audience/scholarly reception, we will consider how authorship is constructed, negotiated, and contested across a filmmaker's body of work. Additionally, we will situate Anderson's cinema within broader cultural and historical contexts, paying particular attention to representations of geographical space, masculinity, whiteness, and aging. How do Anderson's films reveal the anxieties, contradictions, and cultural investments of generation x? Through focusing on authorship, what is uncovered or obscured about the relationship between his film's "artistic vision" and the social worlds in which movies are made, viewed, and received?

course_details.Overview of class: This course surveys the history of animation from its sparse beginnings in the 1900s to its pervasive presence in contemporary visual culture. It will cover influential cultural institutions of the silent era, such as stage performance and print comics, to see how animators adapted these for their new art. Then the commercialization of animation will receive an especially close look, starting with an examination of the industrial practices and themes of the Hollywood studios. The "limited animation" model that arose from the ashes of the studio animation units provides a glimpse into animation practices globally, from Japanese anime to Zagreb festival films to educational films of the Middle East. Modernist aesthetics, especially the idea of "visual music," will help to frame films from independent animators outside the studio system. Yet the studio and limited models also provide a framework for understanding the industrialization of computer animation from Flash to Maya.
course_details.Learning Objectives:
By the end of the course, students will be able to:
• explain the major historical trends and modes of production in animation practice in written discussions of readings
• describe features of character design, layout, color, movement, and line in any given animation in written analyses of films
• describe the connection between common technologies, techniques, and modes of production to the formal features of any given animation in written analyses and oral presentations of regional animation
• describe the persistent challenges animators have faced throughout the history of animation and the various solutions they have implemented via written reflections on animation activities

course_details.Overview of class:
We tend to think of creative works in aesthetic or artistic terms: the way they tell us stories, present us with larger-than-life performers, fill our daily lives with music, or inform us about the world. However, the films, television shows, videogames, and popular recordings that we enjoy are produced, distributed, and marketed using the techniques and strategies of modern industry: that is, show business is just as much about the business as it is the show. This combination of art and industry has long sparked debate about the status of the culture or creative industries, and the ways in which they intermingle art and commerce. What is distinctive about the creative industries as industries? What makes an "authentic" expression within this context? Where does the creativity lie in the complex and collaborative productions of the creative industries? What role do advertising and market research play in shaping creative products? To what degree can audiences take an active role in their experience of creative works? How have technological or regulatory developments influenced the way in which creative products are produced, distributed and consumed? What is the culture of labor in the creative industries, and how can it be made to be more diverse and inclusive? How can media texts be made so that they cross cultural or national boundaries?

This course will address these and other questions through an engagement with scholarship on a range of media industries including film, television, popular music, radio and podcasting, advertising, animation, and digital gaming. The course is designed to provide a historical and theoretical introduction to media industries and to allow students to apply that knowledge to a range of industrial contexts.

Our investigation will highlight several business-oriented career paths that RTVF majors might follow after graduation and will be enriched by conversations with Northwestern alums currently working in those areas.

course_details.Overview of class:
Narrators who are unreliable are a fixture in contemporary storytelling. How can we use our characters' flawed and often untrustworthy perspectives to create suspenseful dramatic and comedic works? In this class, students will use unreliable narration to write a compelling tv pilot, short screenplay, or one-act play.

The course will be workshop-centered with a focus on developing collaborative skills within a writers' room-style environment. Each student will create characters and design stories that generate suspense and/or humor through unreliable narration. There will be weekly assignments, which include writing assignments, readings, presentations, and viewing films/television.

By the end of the quarter, each student will have created a complete short film, tv pilot, or one-act play (22-30 pages). Graduate students may choose to write up to 60 pages.

course_details.Overview of class:
This course will examine problems of performance for camera in both documentary practice and documentary techniques in creating and/or capturing performance for fiction. For undergraduate students focused on screen acting, the class offers an opportunity to practice at performance for camera and in rehearsal/workshop conditions, both in collaboration with graduate students more experienced with filmmaking than performance. Exercises will be structured as opportunities for MFA and undergraduate students to learn from one other from perspectives of filmmaker and performer. With the awareness that documentary subjects often perform for camera as much as actors do in fictional films, we will screen and discuss films in class, using traditional dramatic scene analysis to consider issues and techniques of performance in both fiction and documentary. What can actors learn from documentaries? What can documentarians learn from performance in fictional narratives?

We will begin with documentary and anti-illusionistic practices from the theater, such as the living newspaper and neo-futurism, moving on to traditional documentary work complicated by the performances of subjects, documentary re-enactments, and devised fictional narratives. Assignments require students to work on both sides of the camera and to perform live acting exercises in class, though undergraduates will spend more time in front of camera.
course_details.Learning Objectives: Skills developed and evaluated will be regular performance practice for audience and camera, as well as dramatic scene analysis of fiction and documentary performance. Students will both perform and direct performance for assignments. Assignments will include live performance in class and short sketches and films to be shot out of class, as well as leading and participating in discussion of films shown in-class. As in-class critique, discussion, and performance of scenes are essential to the subject matter, class participation will be particularly emphasized.

course_details.Overview of class: This class will introduce students to three modes of interacting with archival media: research-based inquiry, public curation, and creative practice. The course will begin with an introduction to major audiovisual media formats and the challenges of preserving, accessing, exhibiting, and creatively manipulating them. Throughout the quarter, students will gain familiarity with a range of archival institutions and collections in the region, from long-standing private organizations such as Media Burn, Chicago Filmmakers, and the Chicago Film Archive, to university-supported initiatives such as the South Side Home Movie Project and Indiana University's Black Film Center/Archive. Students will learn how to conceptualize research topics, navigate collections, approach archivists, and arrange visits to media collections. Guest speakers will offer personal perspectives on how to write about, program, and creatively reuse archival media, whether working with home movies and personal archives or licensing from major commercial and educational repositories. A series of case studies will examine the social, historical, and political realities that condition how media objects are stored and circulated: what happens, for instance, to the state film archive of Yugoslavia when the nation no longer exists, and how have artists intervened to make this situation visible? What tools - technical, intellectual, aesthetic - do they use to bring these stories back to light? By the end of the class, students will have gained exposure to a range of theories and practical methods of archival activation, and will have an opportunity to complete a research project, propose a public program, or present a work of creative reuse for their final assignment.

course_details.Overview of class: How do we construct/perform our identities in digital spaces? What are the affordances and limitations of digital community building? How do the biases embedded in the technology industry shape who we can be online? Drawing on the field of digital media studies, students will explore these questions from a range of critical viewpoints, including feminist, queer, critical race, and ability perspectives. We will begin the course with a brief discussion of identity and the politics of belonging, before considering the ways in which Millennials and Generation Z have been "born into" digital worlds and how this has shaped contemporary social and cultural relations. Using this foundation, we will cover topics such as influencer culture, hashtag activism & social justice movements, surveillance and more across platforms including TikTok, Instagram, and X. In addition to noting the potential of digital media in creating more just futures, we will also consider the limitations of digital empowerment and the persistence of networked discrimination in online spaces.
course_details.Learning Objectives:
• Identify and explore major themes and ideas related to digital media studies
• Develop a critical vocabulary and media literacy skills necessary for the study of identity and community in digital spaces
• Gain an understanding of various qualitative methodological approaches to the study of digital identities and the ethical concerns central to studying new media
• Apply these skills to a range of case studies that consider digital identities from feminist, queer, critical race, and ability perspectives

course_details.Overview of class: When we consider the subject of children's media culture, we quickly discern a host of contradictory behaviors and attitudes: childhood is seen as a period of timeless wonder, but children are bombarded with all the latest fads and newest gadgets; we try to insulate children from the adult world, but provide them with media technologies that allow them easy access to it; we want kids to be kids, but are thrilled to introduce them to the consumer marketplace through toys, advertisements, and media franchises. This class will explore contradictions such as these by placing discourses around childhood and children's media within their broader cultural, social, and historical contexts. We will discuss a wide range of media texts, including film adaptations of fairy tales and children's literature, children's television, digital games, children's music, online video, and interactive toys. These case studies will allow us to engage with debates about contemporary media culture and interrogate differing perspectives on the nature of childhood. Children are often understood to be a particularly vulnerable segment of the media audience, and the investigation of children's media has much to tell us about regimes of regulation and censorship, theories about media influence on behavior and identity, the relationship between media and the lived environment, and debates about the media's role in education and marketing. Our goal is to better understand children's media culture and the social institutions and practices that have shaped it, while engaging with this important cultural field through critical, historical, and aesthetic analysis.

course_details.Overview of class: This seminar focuses on the choices, methods, and stakes of writing a history of moving images, taking as its starting point the field of useful media: scientific and popular science films, classroom and educational media, sponsored and industrial films, public-health and training videos. Useful media is an especially productive site for historiographic training because the conventional approaches and sources of film history (auteurs, close analysis, the familiar archives of trade and fan discourse) do not easily apply: authorship is collective or unknown, film style is less helpful than it appears, and the literature for any given media text is as varied as the motivations of its sponsors. Topics might include authorship and sponsorship; the use and re-use of footage across institutional contexts; the colonial and global circulation of instructional media; and the politics of the archive. Students will practice dealing with fragmented or non-extant sources, reading primary source material in unfamiliar disciplines, and analyzing the role of aesthetics and medium specificity in works whose primary goal is pedagogical or procedural. "Historiography" in our field often means one's critical orientation toward media history, but it also implies a set of methodological practices. This seminar will ask students to consider how each sense shapes the other.

course_details.Overview of class:
This is the first class in a two-course sequence, where we creatively interrogate how mental illness/health has been represented on screen. Students will develop a nuanced understanding of the underlying issues and media representations and will apply these critical insights towards their own creative projects. Information provided by guest speakers and film screenings will be balanced with students' work on their own creative projects that center on mental health. These projects may take any form, including fiction, documentary, animation, experimental, docu-fiction/hybrid, essay film, video installations, and more. Diversity of storytelling, perspective, form, style, genre, and even technology are all supported. Regular feedback will aid students in taking their projects through the development, writing and production phase with the goal of reaching a stringout or assembly cut by the end of the quarter. The connected second course will be offered during the Spring quarter and will be dedicated to the post-production phase of students' projects.

This course is affiliated with the Pritzker Pucker Studio Lab (PPSL) - Promotion of Mental Health via Cinematic Arts which will provide funding that is to be applied exclusively towards students' project expenses.
